name: Resveratrol

track.title: Lab & animal
track.line: Mice lived longer only on a high-calorie diet

track.title: Dietary supplement
track.line: Sold as a supplement; not reviewed by FDA

what.text: Resveratrol (3,5,4'-trihydroxystilbene) is a plant compound found in grapes, red wine, some berries and certain roots. It has been studied because it extended lifespan in yeast, worms and flies.

src.label: Semba et al., JAMA Intern Med, 2014 (InCHIANTI)

what.text: Researchers proposed it acts on sirtuins (SIRT1) and AMPK, proteins linked to calorie restriction. A 2012 trial in women found it did not change those targets in muscle or fat.
Resveratrol is sold as a dietary supplement. FDA does not review supplements for safety or effectiveness before sale. No trial has shown that it slows aging in people.

research.text: Resveratrol has been tested in many small human trials; ClinicalTrials.gov lists over 200 studies. The metabolic trials disagree: one small 30-day study in obese men found changes like calorie restriction, while larger and longer trials in women and obese men found none. A large observational study found dietary resveratrol levels were not linked to longer life.
Each is listed below as it was run.

research.title: Obese men, 30 days, 2011

facts.v: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover
11 healthy obese men
30 days of 150 mg a day and 30 days of placebo
Metabolic rate, muscle mitochondria, liver fat, blood sugar and fats, blood pressure

research.found: Resting and sleeping metabolic rate fell. Muscle mitochondrial measures, liver fat, glucose, triglycerides, inflammation markers and systolic blood pressure improved. The authors called the changes calorie-restriction-like.

research.title: Non-obese women with normal blood sugar, 2012

facts.v: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled
Non-obese postmenopausal women with normal glucose tolerance
12 weeks of 75 mg a day
Insulin sensitivity of liver, muscle and fat by clamp; body composition; metabolic rate; blood fats; SIRT1 and AMPK in tissue

research.found: No change in insulin sensitivity, body composition, metabolic rate, blood fats or inflammation markers. Resveratrol did not affect SIRT1, AMPK or related targets in muscle or fat.

research.title: High-dose resveratrol in obese men, 2013

facts.v: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel groups; investigator-initiated
24 obese but otherwise healthy men
4 weeks
Insulin sensitivity by clamp (main outcome); glucose turnover; blood pressure; energy use; body fat; markers

research.found: No effect on insulin sensitivity, glucose, blood pressure, energy use, liver or belly fat, or blood markers. The authors said this raised doubt about resveratrol as a supplement for metabolic disorders.

research.title: Mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, 2015

facts.v: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter (Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study)
119 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's
52 weeks; dose rose from 500 mg a day to 1,000 mg twice a day
Safety; amyloid and tau in blood and spinal fluid; brain volume on MRI; clinical scores

research.found: Resveratrol reached the brain. Amyloid-40 fell less than on placebo. Brain volume loss was greater on resveratrol. Nausea, diarrhea and weight loss were the most common side effects. Results are posted on ClinicalTrials.gov.

research.title: Diet resveratrol and death in older adults (InCHIANTI), 2014

facts.v: Population study in two Chianti villages, 1998 to 2009. Not randomized.
783 community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older
9 years of follow-up
24-hour urine resveratrol metabolites; death from any cause; inflammation; heart disease; cancer

research.found: Urine resveratrol levels were not linked to death, inflammation, heart disease or cancer. 268 people died during follow-up.

src.label: Semba et al., JAMA Intern Med, 2014 (InCHIANTI)

research.text: In middle-aged mice on a high-calorie diet, resveratrol improved health measures and survival. In mice on a standard diet started at 12 months of age, it reduced several signs of aging but did not extend lifespan.

Several animal and lab papers on resveratrol and the heart from one laboratory in Farmington, Connecticut, were retracted by their journals in 2012, for example in Free Radical Biology and Medicine and the American Journal of Physiology. The retraction notices we opened do not state a reason. A 2014 paper from the same group was retracted in 2022 over figure problems the authors could not explain. None of these were human trials.

us.text: Resveratrol is not an FDA-approved drug. It is sold as a dietary supplement, which FDA does not review for safety or effectiveness before sale. A GRAS notice for it was withdrawn before FDA finished its review. As of November 1, 2026.

side.text: In trials, resveratrol was generally well tolerated. In a year-long Alzheimer's trial at high doses, nausea, diarrhea and weight loss were most common, and brain volume fell more than on placebo. FDA does not review supplements for safety before sale.

unconfirmed: We could not open the reason for the 2012 retractions of resveratrol papers from the Farmington, Connecticut laboratory; the retraction notices in PubMed have no text, and we did not find an ORI finding.
We could not confirm resveratrol's status with Health Canada, the UK, EU regulators (EUR-Lex and EFSA refused automated requests) or the TGA.
We could not read the SRT501 multiple myeloma trial (Popat et al., 2013); its PubMed record has no abstract.
We did not count how many resveratrol NDI notifications FDA lists or read FDA's replies.
The 2012 US trial abstract does not give how many women took part.
surprises: Resveratrol is often linked to the 'red wine' longevity story, but in older Italians, resveratrol levels from diet were not linked to living longer.
In mice on a normal diet, resveratrol did not extend lifespan; the lifespan gain was in mice on a high-calorie diet.
In a year-long Alzheimer's trial, brain volume fell more on resveratrol than on placebo.
Resveratrol sits in FDA's 503A Category 1, meaning FDA is still evaluating it for compounding, not that it is approved.
